title: Stowers scientist selected for $28.6 million effort to predict protein changes behind neurodegenerative disease
key_facts: A new research effort provides up to $28.6 million for scientists across the US to train AI to predict when proteins are likely to go wrong in neurodegenerative disease.
The Stowers Institute lab of Randal Halfmann will receive about $4.1 million over two years from ARPA-H to generate large-scale data on protein aggregation.

AI predicts many protein structures, but roughly one-third of proteins have no stable structure (intrinsically disordered proteins), which can clump together in diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS and Huntington's.
Halfmann's lab will measure 50,000 proteins in yeast cells under conditions mimicking ageing, expecting over 10 billion measurements from more than 1 million samples.
The project, NATIVE-ID, is led by the Innovative Genomics Institute at UC Berkeley as part of ARPA-H's BIOGAMI program, with teams from Brown, Emory, Johns Hopkins, Texas A&M and others.
The first focus is frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), related to ALS.
BIOGAMI has two 24-month phases: Phase 1 builds datasets and models; Phase 2 validates potential therapeutics and ways to detect protein dysfunction earlier.
quote_evidence: “If we can better predict the probabilities and onset ages of disease, it could allow many more people to seek preventive or early-stage treatments or enroll in clinical trials,” said Stowers Institute Investigator Randal Halfmann, Ph.D.

Halfmann and his lab will measure the aggregation tendencies of 50,000 proteins, each individually expressed in yeast cells under diverse conditions designed to mimic the things that go wrong in human cells as we age.
The current award funds an initial two-year phase of work.
why_it_matters_hint: A funded plan to build the missing data AI needs to predict harmful protein clumping early.
notes: Institute's own news release (as posted on EurekAlert); ARPA-H and Berkeley pages referenced but not read. Funding is 'up to' $28.6 million.
